newsitem.title: USA: Venezuela leaked S&P ratings upgrade-US investors.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela leaked S&P ratings upgrade-US investors.

text.p: Venezuela's economic team, which came to New York Thursday to update Wall Street on its economic progress, leaked information that Standard & Poors would raise the country's credit rating later in the day, U.S. investors said.

Attendees at a roadshow for Venezuela's upcoming $315 million Eurobond said Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar announced publicly that S&P would raise the country's long-term foreign currency rating to B-plus, from single-B, later that same afternoon.
"Matos actually said we've been trying to improve our relationship with the rating agencies and S&P will upgrade us today, it will appear on the wires," one analyst said.
Some 100 people attended the luncheon. Word of the imminent upgrade spread rapidly through the emerging debt market and had a dramatic impact on prices.
"He actually gave some of us a head start," the analyst said, "The Brady market soared on that."
Prices of Venezuelan Brady bonds bolted higher in early afternoon, so much so that the official release of the upgrade at 1550 EDT/1950 GMT had little affect on prices.

At the close, Venezuela Pars VZ675C20=RR gained one point to 77-1/2, DCBs VZFLL07=RR were up 5/8 to 92, and FLIRBs VZ6C97=RR rose 1-3/4 to bid 92-1/2, with most of the gains made earlier in the day, he said.
One investor said that the news flowed across the roadshow even before Matos made his comments at around 1330 EDT/1730 GMT.
"I talked to 10 people before we sat to lunch (at around noon) and all knew about it," the investor said. "I dont know if they knew because they talked to Matos but they all knew."
"There was a total leak," the investor said.

David Beers, S&P's managing director for sovereign ratings, said S&P followed its standard procedure by informing Venezuela before the rating was changed. He added that all debt issuers understood they were obligated not to comment on a ratings action until it was released.

"Our policy of confidentiality is based upon the recognition that we are dealing with market sensitive information," Beers said "We communicate that to issuers. It's the obligation of the issuer to act appropriately."
Beers said he could not comment on the allegations of a leak from Venezuelan officials. "If there are leaks in the marketplace, they did not come from us."
